         COMES NOW, Cherokee Creek Partners, Bonnie Helene McAnelly, Individually and as

 Trustee of the 2025 Homestead Trust and the Bonnie Helene McAnelly 2023 Trust (“Cherokee

 Creek Aligned Intervenors”) and file their Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) with

 Proposed Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law, and Ordering Paragraphs.

   I.    INTRODUCTION

         Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors wholly agree with the Administrative Law Judges’

 (“ALJs”) primary recommendation: the Application should be denied.            The ALJs correctly

 concluded that this process deprived many landowners of the process due them under 16 Texas

 Administrative Code § 22.52(a)(4), to their prejudice, and that the Application should therefore be

 denied. 1    The Public Utility Commission (“Commission” or “PUC”) should adopt that

recommendation.


          Only if the Commission declines to deny the Application and instead selects a route for

construction do the remaining exceptions apply. Should the Commission reach route selection, it

should not adopt the ALJs’ alternative recommendation of Route 894 and instead should adopt

Route CCG. The ALJs’ recommended decision rests principally on a modest cost differential and

a limited habitable-structures comparison, while giving insufficient weight to the full range of

criteria Texas law requires. PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 Texas Administrative Code §

25.101(b)(3)(B) require a holistic balancing of all statutory and rule factors: community values,

recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, prudent

avoidance, paralleling of compatible corridors, and moderation of impact on affected landowners

and communities. 2 No single factor controls. 3 When all required criteria are weighed, Route

Cherokee Creek G (“Route CCG”) is the route that best balances them, and it is superior to each

of the four routes the ALJs primarily focused on, which were Route 894, Route 487, Route 392,

and Route 296 (the “Focus Routes”).


    II.   THE  COMMISSION  SHOULD    ADOPT    THE                                    ALJs’   PRIMARY
          RECOMMENDATION AND DENY THE APPLICATION.


          The ALJs’ primary recommendation is denial, and the record fully supports it. The Joint

Applicants held three public meetings before filing. 4 After those meetings, they materially

McCulloch Counties, added approximately 400 miles of new route links, and thereby brought

approximately 1,400 additional landowners within the class entitled to direct-mail notice of the

Application and thus increasing the affected-landowner class from roughly 2,800 to roughly

4,200. 5 No further public meeting was held and, furthermore, the project as filed differed

significantly and materially from that which had been presented at the previous meetings. 6 As a

result, no landowner within the expanded study area, and no owner within 500 feet of the centerline

of the newly created links, ever received notice of a public meeting and, therefore, had no

opportunity to identify routing constraints or voice their community values before the Application

was filed, to their prejudice. 7      Rule 22.52(a)(4) exists to guarantee affected landowners a

meaningful opportunity to participate before an application is filed and the routing framework

hardens. The ALJs correctly held that the Joint Applicants’ failure to afford that opportunity to

those prejudiced landowners requires denial of the Application. 8

          Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors respectfully urge the Commission to adopt those

findings and conclusions and deny the Application. The exceptions that follow are presented solely

in the alternative in the event the Commission elects to certify a route notwithstanding the notice

defect.

          AS PRESENTING “NO CLEAR ADVANTAGE.”

            Should the Commission select a route, it should adopt Route CCG. The PFD grouped Route

CCG among routes that “received considerably less discussion than the Focus Routes” and found

that none “present a clear advantage over the Focus Routes overall.” That conclusion does not

withstand the record. Selecting a route is not a matter of which route is more popular or most

discussed amongst the parties; it is the appropriate weighing of the routing factors. Route CCG is

not a peripheral alternative; it is purpose-built by Cherokee Creek’s expert, Rae Lynn Schneider

Reinecke, who reviewed the full universe of 123 alternatives and designed Route CCG to retain

the favorable portions of the Focus Routes while departing from them only where the record

showed a measurable improvement in protecting parks, river crossings, paralleling and

environmental integrity. 9 Plainly stated, it is a good route with noticeable and superior advantages

to the alternatives, including the Focus Routes.

           Each meaningful departure Route CCG makes from the Focus Routes corresponds to a

documented improvement, and the Environmental Assessment’s own data confirms such. Set

against Route CCG, each Focus Route is inferior on balance. Route 894’s advantages on habitable

structures and cost are modest and fall within statistical and engineering margins; its paralleling

advantage rests on property boundaries rather than compatible infrastructure; and it imposes

avoidable, lasting harm on two irreplaceable state parks and sensitive environmental resources.

Route 487 abuts Colorado Bend State Park and carries the greatest riparian and park-foreground

exposure of the Focus Routes. Route 296 endangers a school and a natural-gas compressor station

and crosses twice the cultural resource sites of Route CCG. Route 392 is the longest, most

expensive, and most heavily burdened Focus Route on habitable structures and cultural resources.

IV.     PARALLELING OF COMPATIBLE CORRIDORS DOES NOT FAVOR ANY
        FOCUS ROUTE OVER ROUTE CCG.

        Paralleling does not tip the balance toward any Focus Route. Route 894’s headline

paralleling figure collapses when looked at more closely: it parallels apparent property boundaries

for roughly 91.75 miles but existing transmission lines for only 5.66 miles and public roads for

only 4.45 miles. 10 Route CCG parallels 14.02 miles of existing transmission-line right-of-way,

which is roughly two-and-a-half times more than Route 894 and more than Route 296’s 11.75

miles, and 15.41 miles of public roads and highways, more than triple Route 894’s 4.45 miles and

more than four times Route 487’s 3.75 miles. 11 Staff witness Poole acknowledged that apparent-

property-boundary measures are “less reliable than existing compatible infrastructure” measures

and that evaluating route performance on compatible-infrastructure paralleling alone “would be a

reasonable proposition.” 12 Routes 487 and 392 do parallel more existing transmission line than

Route CCG (22.05 and 23.60 miles, respectively), but they purchase that paralleling only by

incurring the harms detailed above with Route 487 by hugging Colorado Bend State Park, and

Route 392 by becoming the longest (229.02 miles), most expensive ($1.715 billion), and most

Paralleling is a means to the end of reducing new fragmentation and impact; it does not redeem

routes that inflict the very harms the criterion exists to avoid.


 V.      THE HABITABLE-STRUCTURE AND COST DIFFERENTIALS DO NOT
         OUTWEIGH ROUTE CCG’S SUPERIOR PERFORMANCE ACROSS THE
         STATUTORY CRITERIA.

         The ALJs’ recommendation of Route 894, should a route need to be adopted, rests heavily

on habitable-structure count, but that metric does not meaningfully distinguish Route CCG from

the Focus Routes. Route CCG has 105 habitable structures within 500 feet of its centerline, which

is the same count as Route 296 (105), and thirty-one fewer than Route 392 (136). 13 Route CCG

sits squarely in the middle of the Focus Routes being tied with one and better than another outright,

and just nine more than Route 487 (96), and twenty more than Route 894 (85). 14 Importantly,

single-family residences along Route CCG sit an average of 330.85 feet from the centerline,

compared with 310.66 feet along Route 894, so Route CCG places residences farther from the line

and advances prudent avoidance at least as effectively. 15 Moreover, Ms. Reinecke testified without

contradiction that the standard deviation for this criterion across the 123-route universe is

approximately 27 structures, so the twenty-structure gap against Route 894 and the nine-structure

gap against Route 487 both fall within a single standard deviation and are statistically

comparable. 16 A raw headcount is also not a proxy for prudent avoidance, which the Commission

         The cost differential likewise cannot carry the recommendation, and the ALJs said as much.

The four Focus Routes span a narrow $50 million band ($1.665 billion for Route 487, $1.681

billion for Route 894, $1.685 billion for Route 296, and $1.715 billion for Route 392) and the PFD

comparable.” 19 Staff witness John Poole confirmed that the routes fall in a “tight range” and that

cost differences within his 10 percent rule of thumb lack material significance. 20 In fact, Route

392 alone is $50 million more than Route 487, a spread larger than Route CCG’s premium. 21 That

premium falls comfortably within the Joint Applicants’ own 10-to-15 percent engineering

contingency. 22 Having correctly concluded that cost does not distinguish among the routes, the

ALJs cannot consistently invoke Route CCG’s modest additional cost as a reason to reject it.

Because the differential falls within the range of estimation uncertainty, and because this is a

reliability project for which no cost-to-consumers analysis is even required, cost should be treated

 VI.      ROUTE CCG BETTER PROTECTS THE TWO STATE                                         PARKS,
         ENVIRONMENTAL INTEGRITY, AND COMMUNITY VALUES.

         PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(B) requires the Commission to weigh impacts on parks and

recreational areas, and on that criterion, Route CCG is the strongest route in contention. On the

Environmental Assessment’s own metric, being estimated miles of right-of-way within the

foreground visual zone of parks and recreational areas, Route CCG registers 0 miles, tying Route

894 (0 miles) and outperforming Route 296 (0.69 miles), Route 392 (0.73 miles), and, most

dramatically, Staff’s Route 487 (4.25 miles). 24 Route 487 is also the only Focus Route with a park

or recreational area within 1,000 feet of its centerline. 25 Route CCG’s advantage over Route 894,

whose foreground figure is likewise 0, emerges from a distance-band and viewshed analysis: Route

CCG has no park or recreational acreage within the 0.5-to-1-mile band, while Route 894 places

442.65 acres of state-park land in that close-proximity band and 4,871.91 acres in the 1-to-2-mile

band. 26 That is a substantial difference far in favor of Route CCG’s figure. Route 894’s link

sequence would expose the most trails, primary roadways, and both park headquarters to the

visible zone, whereas Route CCG’s Colorado River crossing at Links J31–J32 produces the lowest

overall visibility of any evaluated alignment. 27 Route 487, for its part, runs Segment J11 roughly

100 feet from Colorado Bend State Park’s northern boundary and crosses Colorado Park Road so

that park visitors pass directly under the line. 28

         Furthermore, Route CCG avoids United States Fish and Wildlife Service (“USFWS”)

Karst Zone 1 entirely and avoids the Edwards Aquifer; it avoids the Ecologically Significant

Stream Segment (“ESSS”) portion of the Colorado River and the Rocky Creek ESSS that Route

894 crosses; and it avoids the USFWS-designated critical habitat for the Texas fatmucket

(Lampsilis bracteata). 29 Measured against the Southern-corridor Route 296 and the Northern-

corridor Route 392, the record is more lopsided still: Route CCG crosses only 2 recorded cultural

resource sites (the same as Routes 487 and 894), while Route 296 crosses 4 and Route 392 crosses

16. 30 Route 392 also carries the most recorded cultural resources within 1,000 feet (47, versus 12

for Route 894) and the greatest length across high-probability archaeological areas (64.94 miles). 31

A route that the ALJs themselves described as differing from Route 894 only in its Colorado River

and San Saba River crossings, and that outperforms one or more of the Focus Routes on criterion

after criterion, cannot fairly be dismissed as presenting no clear advantage. The finding should be

rejected.


        Route CCG also better preserves environmental integrity under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D).

J32, farther from both state parks. 32 At the San Saba River, it crosses alongside an existing

already-affected corridor, which is exactly what the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department

(“TPWD”) recommended and what the paralleling criteria are designed to reward. 33 The Focus

        Finally, Route CCG most closely reflects the documented community values in this record.

A review of 3,793 filings comprised of 1,580 unique intervenors, 950 protest forms, and 654

most prioritized minimizing length across residential areas, minimizing the line’s visibility,

maximizing paralleling, and maximizing distance from parks and recreational areas. 37 Route CCG

addresses all four priorities more comprehensively than Route 894, Route 487, Route 296, or Route

392.

 VIII.    CONCLUSION

         The ALJs correctly recommended that the Application be denied, and Cherokee Creek

 Aligned Intervenors urge the Commission to adopt that recommendation. Should the Commission

 instead select a route for construction, the record does not support the ALJs’ alternative

 recommendation of Route 894. The Proposal for Decision recommends Route 894 primarily

 because it costs less and, on its face, has fewer habitable structures. Neither of those facts is

 sufficient enough to override the full spectrum of criteria the Commission is required to weigh,

 and the record supports Route CCG:

         • Route CCG best moderates the impact on the affected community and landowners and
         best balances the routing criteria of PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B),
         with no single factor controlling.
         • Route CCG’s habitable-structure count (105) is tied with Route 296, nine more than
         Route 487, twenty more than Route 894, and thirty-one fewer than Route 392—well within
         one standard deviation of the alternatives—and it places residences farther from the
         centerline on average, advancing prudent avoidance.
         • Route CCG’s cost premium (approximately $40 million, or 2.4%, more than the Focus
         Routes, which themselves span a $50 million band) falls within the Joint Applicants’ own
         10-to-15% engineering contingency, and the ALJs found cost was not a distinguishing
         factor.
         • Route CCG parallels far more existing compatible infrastructure than Route 894 (5.66
         transmission miles) and Route 296, and where Routes 487 and 392 parallel more
         transmission line they do so only by incurring greater park, environmental, habitable-
         structure, and cultural-resource harms.
         • Route CCG records zero miles of right-of-way within the foreground visual zone of
         parks—tying Route 894 and beating Route 296 (0.69), Route 392 (0.73), and Route 487
         (4.25)—and, unlike Route 894, has no park acreage within the 0.5-to-1-mile band, where
         Route 894 places 442.65 acres.
         • Route CCG avoids USFWS Karst Zone 1, the Edwards Aquifer, the ESSS portions
         crossed by Route 894, and the Texas fatmucket critical habitat, and yields approximately
         438 fewer acres of clearing in fragmentation-sensitive habitats and 6.43 fewer miles of
         Golden-cheeked Warbler habitat than Route 894.

I. FINDINGS OF FACT

    Applicants

    1.      Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (Oncor) is a Delaware limited liability
            company registered with the Texas Secretary of State under filing number
            800880712. Oncor owns and operates for compensation in Texas facilities and
            equipment to transmit and distribute electricity in the Electric Reliability Council
            of Texas (ERCOT) region.

    2.      Oncor holds certificate of convenience and necessity (CCN) number 30043 to
            provide service to the public.

    3.      LCRA Transmission Services Corporation (LCRA) is a Texas non-profit
            corporation registered with the Texas Secretary of State under filing number
            159084801. LCRA owns and operates in Texas facilities and equipment to transmit
            electricity in the ERCOT region.

    4.      LCRA provides service under CCN number 30110.

    5.      Oncor and LCRA (collectively, Applicants) filed a joint application in this docket.

    The Joint Application

    6.      On March 26, 2026, Applicants filed a joint application (Application) with the
            Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) to amend their respective CCNs
            to construct, own, and operate the Bell County East-to-Big Hill 765- kilovolt (kV)
            transmission line (the Project) in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano,
            Mason, McCulloch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and
            Williamson Counties, Texas.

    7.      The Commission opened this docket on March 6, 2026; the Application was filed
            20 days later.

    8.      The Project is one of five 765-kV extra-high-voltage transmission lines designated
            in the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP), which ERCOT developed and the
            Commission approved, and together comprise three 765-kV import paths designed
            to transfer large-scale power into the Permian Basin region.
